subject: pe
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes quantitative data?
options: Numerical data that can be measured or counted
Descriptive data based on opinions and feelings
Data that can only be collected by interview
Data that cannot be represented on a graph
questions.explain: Quantitative data is numerical information, such as measurements or counts, that can be recorded as numbers.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes qualitative data?
options: Descriptive, non-numerical data based on opinions or feelings
Numerical data collected using a stopwatch
Data that is always more accurate than numbers
Data that can only be shown in a bar chart
questions.explain: Qualitative data is descriptive and non-numerical, often reflecting opinions, feelings or observations.

questions.q: Objective data is best defined as data that is:
options: Based on facts and measurements, free from personal opinion
Based entirely on a coach's personal judgement
Always qualitative in nature
Impossible to record accurately
questions.explain: Objective data is factual and measurable, so it is not influenced by personal opinion or bias.

questions.q: Subjective data is best defined as data that is:
options: Based on personal opinion or interpretation
Based only on precise measurements
Always numerical and unbiased
Collected only by electronic devices
questions.explain: Subjective data relies on personal opinion or interpretation and can therefore vary between observers.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of quantitative data?
options: A resting heart rate recorded as 62 beats per minute
A coach describing a player as 'determined'
An athlete saying they 'felt tired' after a race
A spectator's opinion that a team played well
questions.explain: A heart rate of 62 bpm is a numerical measurement, making it quantitative data.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of qualitative data?
options: A coach's written description of a player's attitude in a match
The distance of a long jump measured in metres
The number of goals scored in a season
A stopwatch time for a 100m sprint
questions.explain: A written description of attitude is descriptive and non-numerical, so it is qualitative data.

questions.q: Which of the following is most likely to be subjective data?
options: A gymnastics judge's score for the artistry of a routine
The time taken to swim 50 metres
A GPS measurement of distance covered
The number of successful passes in a game
questions.explain: A judgement about artistry depends on personal opinion and interpretation, making it subjective.

questions.q: A fitness tester records an athlete's VO2 max as 55 ml/kg/min. This data is best classified as:
options: Quantitative and objective
Qualitative and subjective
Qualitative and objective
Quantitative and subjective
questions.explain: The VO2 max value is a numerical measurement free from opinion, so it is both quantitative and objective.

questions.q: Which type of graph is most suitable for showing how a variable changes over a period of time?
options: Line graph
Pie chart
Bar chart
Table
questions.explain: A line graph is used to display continuous change over time, such as heart rate during exercise.

questions.q: A bar chart is most commonly used to:
options: Compare the values of separate categories
Show the exact relationship between two continuous variables
Display data as a proportion of a whole circle
Record raw data in rows and columns
questions.explain: Bar charts compare discrete categories, with the height of each bar showing its value.

questions.q: A pie chart is most useful for presenting:
options: Proportions of a total as parts of a whole
Change in a variable over time
The correlation between two variables
A list of raw, unprocessed results
questions.explain: A pie chart divides a circle into segments to show each part as a proportion of the whole.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of using a table to present data?
options: To organise raw data clearly in rows and columns
To show a trend line for two variables
To display proportions of a whole
To calculate averages automatically
questions.explain: Tables organise raw data neatly in rows and columns so it can be read and processed easily.

questions.q: A scatter graph is chosen when a performer wants to show:
options: The relationship or correlation between two variables
How one value changes across time only
The proportion each category takes of a total
A single set of unordered results
questions.explain: Scatter graphs plot paired values to reveal the correlation between two variables.

questions.q: A coach records a swimmer's heart rate every minute during a 20-minute session. Which is the most appropriate way to present this data?
options: A line graph
A pie chart
A single bar
An unordered list
questions.explain: Because heart rate is measured continuously over time, a line graph best shows the trend across the session.

questions.q: A scatter graph shows that as training hours increase, fitness scores also increase. This indicates:
options: A positive correlation
A negative correlation
No correlation
A pie proportion
questions.explain: When both variables rise together, the relationship is described as a positive correlation.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of discrete data?
options: The number of goals scored in a match
The exact time taken to run 400 metres
The height of an athlete in centimetres
The distance of a javelin throw
questions.explain: Discrete data can only take whole-number values, such as a count of goals scored.

questions.q: A line graph shows heart rate rising from 70 bpm at rest to 150 bpm after 5 minutes of exercise. What is the increase in heart rate?
options: 80 bpm
70 bpm
150 bpm
220 bpm
questions.explain: The increase is found by subtracting the resting value from the exercise value: 150 minus 70 equals 80 bpm.

questions.q: A table shows Player A scored 25 goals and Player B scored 10 goals in a season. What conclusion can be correctly drawn from this data?
options: Player A scored more goals than Player B
Player A is a better all-round athlete than Player B
Player B is unfit compared with Player A
Player A trained harder than Player B
questions.explain: Only the goal totals can be compared from the data; broader conclusions about fitness or training are not supported.

specSource: AQA GCSE Physical Education (8582) specification; Use of Data
